source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN Examination, 7th ed.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which breakfast is appropriate for a 6-year-old with celiac disease?
questions.rationale: Gluten is found in wheat, rye, barley, and oats. Rice and corn are gluten-free and serve as substitute grains.
explanations: Pandesal is made from wheat flour.
Correct: rice is gluten-free.
Oats are restricted on a gluten-free diet.
Wheat crackers contain gluten.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 276)
questions.quote: Corn and rice, as well as vegetables, are acceptable in a gluten-free diet, and corn and rice become substitute foods.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client with heart failure about seasoning food at home. Which should the client avoid?
questions.rationale: Sodium causes fluid retention, so clients with heart failure limit high-sodium condiments such as patis, toyo, and bagoong. Citrus, garlic, and pepper add flavor without sodium.
explanations: Correct: fish sauce is very high in sodium.
Calamansi adds flavor without sodium.
Garlic is a sodium-free seasoning.
Pepper is a sodium-free seasoning.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 278)
questions.quote: Clients with heart failure need to monitor sodium intake because sodium causes the retention of fluid.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with hepatic encephalopathy is choosing lunch from the hospital menu. Which item should the nurse advise the client to avoid?
questions.rationale: The damaged liver cannot convert ammonia to urea, so protein and ammonia-containing foods (meat, poultry, cheese, milk) are limited to prevent worsening encephalopathy.
explanations: Vegetables are acceptable.
Fruit is acceptable.
Correct: poultry is a high-protein food that raises ammonia.
Tomato soup is acceptable.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 353)
questions.quote: Clients with hepatic encephalopathy have impaired ability to convert ammonia to urea

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with a new colostomy complains of gas building up in the pouch. Which food should the nurse suggest to help prevent this?
questions.rationale: Yogurt, crackers, and toast help reduce gas. Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, onions, and peas are gas-forming and are avoided until tolerance is known.
explanations: Cabbage is gas-forming.
Broccoli is gas-forming.
Cauliflower is gas-forming.
Correct: yogurt helps reduce flatus.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 354)
questions.quote: Consumption of yogurt, crackers, and toasted bread can help prevent gas.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.situation: Mr. Santos, 58, underwent a subtotal gastrectomy (Billroth II) for a bleeding peptic ulcer. He is now tolerating a soft diet and is preparing for discharge.
questions.stem: Which instruction helps prevent dumping syndrome?
options: Lie down for a while after each meal
Drink two glasses of water with every meal
Eat three large meals a day
Choose sweet desserts for extra energy
questions.rationale: Lying down after meals and avoiding fluids with meals slow gastric emptying. The diet is small, frequent, dry meals high in protein, moderate in fat, and low in carbohydrates, without concentrated sweets.
explanations: Correct: lying down slows emptying into the jejunum.
Fluids with meals speed gastric emptying.
Small, frequent meals are recommended.
Concentrated sweets trigger dumping.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 227)
questions.quote: The client should lie down after eating and avoid drinking liquids with meals to prevent this syndrome.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.situation: Mr. Santos, 58, underwent a subtotal gastrectomy (Billroth II) for a bleeding peptic ulcer. He is now tolerating a soft diet and is preparing for discharge.
questions.stem: Fifteen minutes after lunch, Mr. Santos becomes dizzy, sweaty, and pale and reports palpitations. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Early dumping occurs 5 to 30 minutes after eating as food rushes into the jejunum, causing vasomotor symptoms: dizziness, sweating, pallor, tachycardia, and palpitations.
explanations: A leak causes pain, fever, and signs of peritonitis.
Ileus causes distention and absent bowel sounds.
Correct: vasomotor symptoms soon after eating are typical.
Pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 367)
questions.quote: Early manifestations of dumping syndrome occur 5 to 30 minutes after eating.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which finding should the nurse expect in a client with cholecystitis?
options: Pain in the left lower quadrant
questions.rationale: Blocked bile flow causes clay-colored stools, dark urine, and possible steatorrhea. Pain is in the upper right abdomen, may radiate to the right shoulder, and is triggered by fatty meals.
explanations: Urine becomes dark, not pale.
Correct: lack of bile pigment lightens the stool.
Tarry stools suggest upper GI bleeding.
Gallbladder pain is in the right upper quadrant.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 558)
questions.quote: pain triggered by a high-fat meal; clay-colored stools, dark urine, and possible steatorrhea

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with a ruptured appendix is being monitored for peritonitis. Which finding supports this complication?
questions.rationale: Peritonitis causes a distended, rigid, boardlike abdomen, diminished bowel sounds, and inability to pass flatus or stool, along with fever and tachycardia.
explanations: Tachycardia, not bradycardia, is expected.
Fever, not low temperature, is expected.
Bowel sounds diminish.
Correct: abdominal rigidity is a classic sign.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 562)
questions.quote: a rigid, boardlike abdomen; diminished bowel sounds

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse give a client with chronic pancreatitis to prevent exacerbations?
options: Eat high-fat meals to regain weight
Take three large meals a day
questions.rationale: Exacerbations are prevented by avoiding alcohol, nicotine, and caffeine and by eating small, bland, low-fat, high-protein meals.
explanations: Correct: alcohol is a major trigger.
Fat stimulates pancreatic secretion and should be limited.
Small, frequent meals are recommended.
Caffeinated drinks should be avoided.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 556)
questions.quote: avoiding alcohol ingestion, nicotine, and caffeinated beverages

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with diabetes mellitus has a blood glucose of 644 mg/dL. Which acid-base imbalance is the client at risk of developing?
questions.rationale: Without enough insulin, cells break down fat for fuel. Ketones from fat metabolism are acids, which can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis.
explanations: Hyperventilation may occur as compensation, but it is not the primary imbalance.
Ketones lower pH; they do not raise it.
Correct: ketoacids cause metabolic acidosis.
The primary problem is metabolic, not respiratory.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 216)
questions.quote: Diabetes mellitus can lead to metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.situation: Aling Nena, 52, took prednisone bought without a prescription for her joint pains for several months. She is admitted with a moon face, buffalo hump, and thin skin and is diagnosed with Cushing's syndrome.
questions.stem: Which intervention should the nurse include to detect a common complication of her condition?
questions.rationale: Excess glucocorticoids raise blood glucose and can produce signs of diabetes mellitus, so glucose is monitored. Fragile bones and muscle wasting make vigorous exercise unsafe.
explanations: Cortisol, not epinephrine, is the hormone in excess.
Correct: hyperglycemia is a common complication.
Osteoporosis and muscle wasting make vigorous exercise unsafe.
Protein is needed to counter muscle wasting.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 398)
questions.quote: increased levels of glucocorticoids can result in hyperglycemia and signs and symptoms of diabetes mellitus.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.situation: Aling Nena, 52, took prednisone bought without a prescription for her joint pains for several months. She is admitted with a moon face, buffalo hump, and thin skin and is diagnosed with Cushing's syndrome.
questions.stem: Her daughter says that Aling Nena now cries easily, forgets things, and cannot concentrate. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: 'This shows she is depressed about being in the hospital.'
'These are early signs of dementia unrelated to her illness.'
'This happens when her blood sugar drops too low.'
'Excess cortisol can cause mood and memory changes.'
questions.rationale: Exaggerated glucocorticoid effects in Cushing's syndrome cause mood disturbances, memory loss, and poor concentration.
explanations: This ignores a known effect of her disorder.
These changes are linked to her cortisol excess.
Cushing's causes high, not low, blood glucose.
Correct: mood and cognitive changes are features of Cushing's syndrome.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 406)
questions.quote: This exaggerated physiological action can cause mood disturbances

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client is scheduled for bilateral adrenalectomy. What should the nurse tell the client about care after surgery?
options: 'You will need adrenal hormone replacement for life.'
'Your hormones will return to normal in a few weeks.'
'You will need a diet very low in sodium for life.'
questions.rationale: Removing both adrenal glands eliminates cortisol and aldosterone production, so replacement is permanent. Afterward the client is watched for acute adrenal insufficiency.
explanations: Correct: without adrenal glands, replacement is lifelong.
The tumor is usually benign; chemotherapy is not routine.
No adrenal tissue remains to recover.
Loss of aldosterone causes sodium loss, so severe restriction is not the plan.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 408)
questions.quote: Clients undergoing a bilateral adrenalectomy require permanent replacement of adrenal hormones.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: To prevent Addisonian crisis, which medication does the nurse expect to give in the immediate preoperative period before an adrenalectomy?
questions.rationale: A parenteral glucocorticoid such as methylprednisolone is given just before adrenalectomy to protect against acute adrenal insufficiency.
explanations: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid used for later maintenance.
Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist, not a replacement.
Correct: an IV glucocorticoid prevents adrenal crisis.
Potassium does not prevent adrenal insufficiency.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 409)
questions.quote: Methylprednisolone sodium succinate protects the client from developing acute adrenal insufficiency (Addisonian crisis)

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which position helps prevent increased intracranial pressure in a client with a head injury?
options: Left Sims' position with knees flexed
Head of bed at 30 degrees, head midline
Flat with the head on a small pillow
questions.rationale: The head of the bed is raised at least 30 degrees with the head midline and neutral, avoiding extreme neck and hip flexion, to promote venous drainage from the brain.
explanations: Side-lying with flexion can impede venous return.
Correct: elevation with a midline head promotes venous drainage.
Lying flat raises ICP.
Head-down positions raise ICP.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 372)
questions.quote: The head of the bed is elevated to at least 30 degrees or as recommended by the primary health care provider.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: An unconscious client with a head injury shows rigid extension of the arms and legs with the wrists pronated. The nurse recognizes this as a sign of:
options: Flaccid paralysis from a spinal injury
Decorticate posturing from a cortical lesion
Decerebrate posturing from a brainstem injury
questions.rationale: Decerebrate posturing, with abnormal involuntary extension, can occur with upper brainstem injury. Decorticate posturing is flexion of the arms. Either one signals deterioration and must be reported at once.
explanations: Flaccidity is a lack of muscle tone, not rigid extension.
Decorticate posturing is flexion of the arms, wrists, and fingers.
Abnormal posturing is never a normal response.
Correct: extension posturing points to upper brainstem injury.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 351)
questions.quote: Decerebrate posturing, which can occur with upper brainstem injury, is characterized by abnormal involuntary extension of the extremities.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which intervention in the care plan of a client with a T3 spinal cord injury helps prevent autonomic dysreflexia?
questions.rationale: Autonomic dysreflexia is triggered by bladder or bowel distention or painful skin stimuli. A regular bowel program removes a common trigger.
explanations: Correct: preventing bowel distention removes a trigger.
Turning every 2 hours is needed to prevent pressure injuries.
Fluid restriction concentrates urine and does not prevent distention.
Room temperature is not the main trigger.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 424)
questions.quote: may be triggered by bladder distention, bowel distention, visceral distention, or stimulation of pain receptors in the skin.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis had a chest infection and missed several doses of pyridostigmine. The client now has trouble swallowing and breathing. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Myasthenic crisis follows undermedication, infection, or sudden withdrawal of anticholinesterase drugs. Cholinergic crisis follows overmedication.
explanations: Cholinergic crisis follows too much medication.
GBS is a separate ascending paralysis, often after infection.
Correct: missed doses and infection precipitate myasthenic crisis.
Autonomic dysreflexia occurs with spinal cord injury.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 417)
questions.quote: Myasthenic crisis is caused by undermedication or can be precipitated by an infection or sudden withdrawal of anticholinesterase medications.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client has anterior cord syndrome. Which instruction BEST reduces the client's long-term risk of injury?
options: Test bath water temperature before bathing
Use a vibrating massager on the legs
questions.rationale: Anterior cord syndrome causes loss of motor function and of pain and temperature sensation below the injury, while touch, position, and vibration sense are kept. The client cannot feel burns.
explanations: Orthostatic precautions do not address the main sensory loss.
Position sense is preserved.
Correct: loss of temperature sensation puts the client at risk of burns.
Vibration sense is preserved and is not a safety issue.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 440)
questions.quote: loss of motor function, temperature sensation, and pain sensation below the level of injury.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: After open reduction of a leg fracture and cast application, which finding is the nurse's HIGHEST priority?
options: Pain unrelieved by opioids, with numb toes
A warm, damp cast in the first hour
The client cannot void in the first 4 hours
questions.rationale: Compartment syndrome is the top concern after casting. Numbness, tingling, poor nail-bed blanching, and pain unrelieved by opioids signal compromised circulation.
explanations: Itching is common and not urgent.
Correct: these are signs of compartment syndrome.
A new plaster cast is normally warm while it sets.
Retention needs attention but is less urgent than limb ischemia.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 169)
questions.quote: pain that will not be relieved by opioids

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which finding in a client in Buck's traction indicates a complication?
options: Warm toes with brisk capillary refill
Weak pedal pulses on the affected leg
questions.rationale: Buck's traction is skin traction held with an elastic bandage or boot. Weak pedal pulses mean the wrap is compressing the vessels. Skin traction has no pins.
explanations: Some discomfort is expected.
This is a normal circulatory finding.
Buck's is skin traction and has no pins.
Correct: weak pulses show vascular compromise.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 163)
questions.quote: Weak pedal pulses are a sign of vascular compromise
